text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has prepared public opinion and financial markets carefully for an audit of public finances to be published on Monday and for the accompanying tax and savings measures.

Jospin is well positioned to blame his conservative predecessor, Alain Juppe, for a 1997 deficit expected to be running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, and to explain why big business, rather than ordinary taxpayers, should bear the brunt of deficit-reduction.

The measures to be announced by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Monday will come as no shock and are unlikely to put an end to Jospin's honeymoon, illustrated by a 48 percent approval rating in an Ifop public opinion poll published on Sunday.

Political analysts say the real test for the left-wing government will come in September when it has to produce a credible 1998 budget meeting the three percent deficit limit set by the European Union's Maastricht treaty for countries taking part in the 1999 launch of a single currency while starting to keep its promises to create French jobs and cut working hours without loss of pay.

The CNPF employers' federation has protested that the government cannot raise corporate tax to 40 percent from 36.6 percent and at the same time expect industry to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs for the unemployed.

Government sources said Strauss-Kahn would argue that big companies, whose profits are at a record high, had enjoyed five years of handouts and tax breaks from right-wing governments yet had continued to reduce their workforces.
What business needs to create jobs is stronger demand, and thus more consumer spending, ministers say.
That will enable the Socialist premier to keep his promise to left-wing voters that there will be "no new austerity" this year to qualify France for the single EU currency in 1999.
Yet, despite the forecast return of healthier economic growth, it will be harder to make ends meet in 1998 without serious reductions in public spending, economists say.

A leaked handover memo from Juppe written after Jospin's upset in the June 1 national assembly election, acknowledged a revenue shortfall of at least 35 billion francs ($5.8 billion) this year and said that without new measures, next year's deficit would be 4.0 percent of GDP.

The leaking of that note has made it harder for Juppe or new Gaullist opposition leader Philippe Seguin to contest the audit and has triggered fresh recrimination among the Gaullists over who was to blame for their humiliating defeat.
Conservative President Jacques Chirac acknowledged in a television interview last week that the centre-right coalition had left a deficit running at about 3.5 percent.
He appeared to admit what Juppe had denied during the April-May parliamentary election campaign: that the ousted government had been planning a new wave of spending cuts as soon as the poll was over.

The prospect of a higher tax burden on companies -- the government is also weighing extra levies on capital gains and/or an increase in employers' pension contributions -- knocked more than three percent off share prices last Thursday and Friday.

But there too, Jospin could be lucky. The Paris Bourse has risen by about 50 percent in the last year and the reimbursement this month of the "Balladur bond" raised in 1993 freed up some 60 billion francs, much of which is likely to be invested in shares, dealers say.
The government has used news management skills in softening up the public and markets for bad news on the deficit by lowering expectations gradually.

Jospin said in a June 19 maiden policy speech to parliament that the state of public finances was "serious". Strauss-Kahn then said in late June that France would not make "3.0" percent, or 3.1 for that matter. Since then, the slippage in expectations on the deficit has been roughly one-tenth of one percentage point per week.

In contrast to his omnipresent predecessor, Jospin has mainly stayed out of the front line, allowing ministers to do most of the presentational work, at which both Strauss-Kahn and Social Solidarity Minister Martine Aubry are skilled.
The prime minister has only given one television interview, made few public speeches and projected an image of modesty and patience far from Juppe's "uptight-technocrat-in-a-hurry" style.

Jospin has applied the same news management techniques to gradually shedding the left's campaign "no privatisation" stance in favour of a case-by-case acceptance of some selloffs to raise needed cash without angering his Communist coalition partners.

It is now widely expected that the state will sell a minority stake in France Telecom, reduce its shareholding in arms maker Thomson-CSF to a blocking minority and gradually divest from banks and insurance companies. ($ = 6.055 French Francs)
